newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania President offers help, but refunds a farce.
newsitem.headline: Albania President offers help, but refunds a farce.

text.p: President Sali Berisha pledged on Tuesday limited help for impoverished Albanians who poured life savings into failed investment schemes, but the start of a partial refund scheme quickly degenerated into farce.

Only a handful of savers promised a refund of 60 percent of funds ploughed into one scheme received money from designated kerb-side booths. Many people did not appear on official lists, others refused to accept less than their entire stake.

"I put $40,000 into this fund and want $40,000 back, not $24,000," said Stavrula Shehu, a young woman who invested all the money sent to her by relatives abroad. "If I accept their 60 percent, I can't hope for any more."
More than 150,000 people are believed to have invested in the Populli fund, and by nightfall bank staff at two of the nine booths said only 21 people had collected money.

Berisha said a meeting of political parties and trade unions had agreed to provide housing for gullible Albanians who sold their homes to invest the cash. But he said his government could not provide blank cheques.
"The government must not adopt inflationary measures and must not print money. Misfortune should not be cured with misfortune," Berisha, founder of the rightist Democratic Party, told reporters.

He rejected charges that his government had failed to warn investors emerging from eastern Europe's most repressive communist regime. Virtually every family in the country of 3.4 million put money into the schemes.
Five schemes have folded, but compensation has been announced for only two whose assets were frozen in state banks. A 52 percent refund was due to start on Wednesday for a second investment plan.

The head of a third scheme popular in southern towns admitted on Tuesday his operation had collapsed and urged investors to be patient in reclaiming refunds promised for later this week in the Adriatic port of Vlore.
"I ask investors not to come to reclaim their savings. I have no money," Fitim Gerxhalliu said on state television. "I tried but failed. I am trying now to cash in some assets."
It was by no means certain that fresh protests would erupt after a recent crackdown against demonstrators who set fire to public buildings last month over the collapse of the schemes.
Nearly 150 people were arrested and prosecutors are seeking long jail terms on rioting charges. Many would-be demonstrators were prompted to stay away from new rallies last weekend.
The police appeared to be taking no chances of new outbursts in the more volatile south and set up roadblocks in the Vlore region to try to prevent outsiders from entering.

Albania's main opposition groups, which boycotted the talks chaired by Berisha, renewed calls for the government to resign and demanded the release of people jailed in the protests. They asked the United States and European Union "to use their influence to restore democracy in Albania".
"The Albanian people lived under a dictatorship for 40 years and it isn't so difficult to frighten them," said Rexhep Mejdani, the leader of the main opposition Socialist party.

Berisha's Democratic Party, first elected in 1992, backs market reforms and until last year had one of the best records for growth among ex-communist countries. It won a new term last year in polls criticised as unfair by Western observers.
